claim: The trimtab: 'a life-or-death problem solved by one well-placed mechanical intervention rather than more force' (§ The life that shaped the thought), 'trimtab the whole ship with a rudder the size of my hand' (the closing voice) — and § Where he can't see: '"do more with less" has no brake … his story is all reinforcing loops and no balancing one — the efficiency he wins gets reinvested into more consumption, not banked as slack (the Jevons paradox).'

pieces.section: The life that shaped the thought
pieces.what: A ship-and-rudder model: a hull with yaw inertia and drag, a rudder the water flow loads, and a trimtab on the rudder's trailing edge. The walk: turn the ship by pushing the rudder directly and read the effort (torque integrated over the turn); then add the trimtab and turn the ship by moving only the tab, the flow turning the rudder. The test: the trimtab's leverage measured as the ratio of effort to reach the same heading change in the same time, with the measure and the ratio that would mean 'no leverage' (≤ 1) stated before the run. Then the cost the page's own doubt points at — the delay a trimtab adds — read off the same run. A model's numbers, named as the model's; nothing of Fuller's reproduced.
pieces.walks_up_from: a hull drifting with no rudder at all

pieces.what: A doing-more-with-less model: one resource stock, a use rate, and an efficiency that improves each cycle (ephemeralization as a reinforcing loop). Two runs side by side: efficiency gains banked as slack (use falls), and gains spent (the rebound: lower cost per unit, more units). The page's doubt gets its number — with what rebound fraction total use stops falling and starts rising, in this model — and the reader moves the fraction and watches the stock. The verdict rule is stated first: the page's claim ('no balancing loop … gets spent, not banked') is confirmed only if the spent arm consumes more than the banked arm at the model's own ceiling; the piece says what would have meant the page was wrong.
pieces.walks_up_from: one stock drawn down at a fixed rate
